# Reconstructing the Wirecard Public-Fraud Trail

## Executive assessment

The evidence supplied supports a clear reconstruction of a public-fraud warning trail involving Wirecard’s financial reporting, third-party acquiring (“TPA”) revenues, escrow-account balances, audit limitations, and supervisory failures. It does **not**, however, provide evidence sufficient to reconstruct Jan Marsalek’s disappearance, identify his location, establish his role in any disappearance-related conduct, or connect him to the missing funds. Those matters must therefore remain outside the factual conclusions of this report.

The central evidentiary problem is the sharp conflict between Wirecard’s public messaging on 28 April 2020 and the subsequent collapse of the company’s financial position. Wirecard stated that KPMG had found no incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery and that no significant findings required adjustments to the 2016–2018 accounts. At the same time, the company acknowledged that KPMG had not obtained all data required for a forensic verification of important revenues and relied heavily on data relating to December 2019 rather than on independently verified historical evidence. ([Wirecard AG, 2020](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation))

The European Parliament study presents the more consequential interpretation: KPMG could neither confirm nor refute key allegations concerning the TPA business, while approximately €1 billion in trust-account balances could not be verified. In June 2020, Wirecard acknowledged that €1.9 billion in reported bank balances probably did not exist, refused to sign off its 2019 accounts, and filed for insolvency. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

In my assessment, the evidence supports the conclusion that Wirecard’s public-fraud trail was not a single isolated accounting failure. It was a systemic breakdown across corporate disclosures, internal governance, external auditing, financial-reporting enforcement, and market supervision. The evidence is strongest concerning institutional failure and unreliable verification of reported assets and revenues. It is weaker concerning the precise mechanics of the alleged fraud and insufficient, in the supplied material, concerning Jan Marsalek’s disappearance.

## Sources and evidentiary scope

For clarity, this report assigns two source IDs to the supplied materials:

| Source ID | Description | Evidentiary character |
|---|---|---|
| **S1** | Wirecard AG ad hoc announcement dated 28 April 2020 concerning KPMG’s special investigation | Primary company statement; potentially self-interested |
| **S2** | Langenbucher, Leuz, Kra hnen, and Pelizzon, *What are the wider supervisory implications of the Wirecard case?*, European Parliament Economic Governance Support Unit, 2020 | Independent policy study synthesizing public records and cited investigations |

S1 is particularly important for reconstructing what Wirecard told the market. S2 is more useful for evaluating that statement against the later timeline and for identifying supervisory weaknesses. S2 itself cautions against hindsight bias and states that its factual overview is based on public information and is not comprehensive. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

## Chronology of the public-fraud trail

### Early warnings and recurring allegations

The supplied evidence indicates that concerns about Wirecard’s accounting practices predated the 2020 collapse by many years. S2 records allegations dating to 2008, including claims that Wirecard reported unusually high margins and treated customer deposits as its own cash. It also identifies a 2016 report known as the Zatarra Report, which accused Wirecard of corruption, fraud, and money laundering. These were allegations, not adjudicated findings in the supplied material. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The Financial Times began publishing its “House of Wirecard” reporting from 2015 onward. According to S2, employees in Singapore later provided internal documents to journalists because they believed an internal investigation had been suppressed. This is significant because it shows that warnings came from multiple channels: journalists, short sellers, analysts, employees, and other market participants. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The evidence does not establish that every early allegation was accurate. However, the accumulation of warnings should have increased the need for independent verification of Wirecard’s revenue, cash, and third-party relationships.

### 2019: escalation of scrutiny and regulatory intervention

On 30 January 2019, the Financial Times reported allegations involving forged and backdated contracts and Wirecard’s Singapore operations. On 15 February, BaFin directed Germany’s Financial Reporting Enforcement Panel, or FREP, to examine Wirecard’s interim accounts as of 30 June 2018. Four days later, BaFin prohibited the establishment or increase of net short positions in Wirecard shares until 18 April 2019. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

This sequence illustrates a major supervisory tension. Critical reporting and short selling were treated partly as potential threats to market confidence, while the underlying allegations against Wirecard were not resolved promptly. S2 argues that the short-selling ban may have impaired the market’s ability to incorporate negative information into prices. The authors specifically describe short selling as an information channel and recommend that restrictions be limited to circumstances involving market-wide or systemic risk. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

In October 2019, Wirecard hired KPMG to conduct a special forensic investigation. The investigation was publicly framed as a response to accusations in the press and online. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

### March and April 2020: reassuring public statements

On 22 April 2020, Wirecard announced that the KPMG investigation would continue until 27 April and stated that the analysis so far had provided no evidence of balance-sheet manipulation. The 28 April announcement repeated this reassuring position after Wirecard received the report. ([Wirecard AG, 2020](https://www.wirecard.com/2020/04/22/wirecard-ag-kpmg-special-review-lasts-until-april-27-2020-analysis-so-far-provides-no-evidence-of-balance-sheet-manipulation))

The 28 April statement made several specific claims:

1. No incriminating evidence of balance-sheet forgery had been identified.
2. No significant findings in the TPA, merchant-cash-advance/digital-lending, India, or Singapore areas required adjustment of the 2016–2018 accounts.
3. Existing audit work was described as sufficient to prove TPA revenues.
4. KPMG nevertheless had not obtained all data that would have been required under enhanced forensic standards.
5. More than 200 million data sets relating to December 2019 had reportedly been provided to KPMG.
6. That December 2019 review allegedly found no deviations between reported revenues and account balances.
7. Documentation and organizational weaknesses had been identified, but Wirecard said it was remedying them.

These claims were materially qualified by the limitations described in the same announcement. The company acknowledged that important data were controlled by third parties and that the forensic requirements were not fully satisfied for the historical period. Thus, “no evidence identified” did not necessarily mean “all allegations disproved.” It could also mean that the investigation was unable to reach a definitive conclusion because evidence was unavailable or incomplete.

S2 confirms this distinction. It states that KPMG could neither confirm nor refute the allegations and was unable to verify approximately €1 billion in foreign trust accounts. The TPA partners did not cooperate adequately, and there were no official bank confirmations or official statements of account available to the investigation. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

## Audit uncertainty and missing cash

The most important contradiction in the record is between Wirecard’s interpretation of the KPMG review and the evidentiary limitations described in the broader public record.

| Issue | Wirecard’s public presentation | Evidence summarized by S2 | Assessment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Balance-sheet manipulation | No incriminating evidence identified | KPMG could not confirm or refute central allegations | The company’s statement was not equivalent to exoneration |
| TPA revenues | Existing audit measures were said to prove revenues | Historical data required for forensic verification were unavailable or controlled by third parties | Revenue verification remained incomplete |
| Trust accounts | No direct adverse conclusion in S1 | Approximately €1 billion could not be verified; later €1.9 billion was probably nonexistent | Cash evidence was critically unreliable |
| Audit quality | EY had issued clean opinions for earlier years | S2 questions how escrow balances were verified and notes that EY did not refuse the 2019 opinion until 2020 | Audit assurance failed to protect investors |
| Internal controls | Weaknesses were acknowledged as remediable | S2 describes weaknesses in internal controls, oversight, and information flow | Problems were structural, not merely administrative |

S2 reports that EY issued unqualified opinions for Wirecard’s 2015–2018 financial statements, despite earlier public allegations. It further reports that KPMG questioned whether certain escrow balances were appropriately classified as cash or cash equivalents under IFRS. The study also summarizes allegations that EY relied on confirmations issued in the name of a trustee rather than directly obtaining independent confirmation from the relevant bank. These are reported allegations and criticisms in S2, not findings independently established by the two supplied sources. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The sequence became decisive in June 2020. S2 records that Wirecard’s board stated on 22 June that the €1.9 billion in trust-account balances probably did not exist. On 25 June, Wirecard filed for insolvency after EY refused to sign off the 2019 accounts. S2 also records EY’s statement that there were clear indications of a sophisticated fraud involving multiple parties and deliberate deception. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The evidence therefore supports a careful conclusion: the missing cash was not merely an accounting classification dispute. By June 2020, the company itself had acknowledged that the reported balances probably did not exist. The evidence does not, however, fully establish in these materials who created the false confirmations, how the funds were allegedly represented, or the complete chain of responsibility.

## Supervisory and governance failures

S2 identifies five failed lines of defence:

1. Wirecard’s internal control system.
2. The supervisory board.
3. External audit.
4. Oversight bodies for financial reporting and auditing.
5. BaFin as market supervisor.

The institutional design problem was particularly important. Germany used a two-step financial-reporting enforcement structure in which FREP carried out the first stage and BaFin retained enforcement responsibility. FREP depended significantly on company cooperation and lacked the same statutory investigative powers as a public authority. S2 argues that this structure created latency, unclear responsibility, and an excessive reliance on voluntary information. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

S2 also states that BaFin’s role was complicated because Wirecard’s parent company was not treated as a bank or financial holding company, even though the group included a bank subsidiary. This limited the direct banking-supervision tools available at the parent-company level. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

The study’s recommendations included:

- stronger protection and incentives for whistleblowers;
- more restrictive use of short-selling bans;
- explicit statutory requirements for auditor skepticism and fraud-focused checks;
- higher auditor liability;
- greater transparency concerning audit-oversight findings;
- mandatory effective internal-control systems for listed companies;
- stronger independent audit committees;
- making BaFin the sole competent authority for financial-reporting enforcement;
- stronger investigative powers under the Transparency Directive; and
- creation of a European Single Capital Market Supervisor.

These are policy recommendations, not evidence that the reforms were adopted or that they would necessarily have prevented the fraud. ([Langenbucher et al., 2020](https://safe-frankfurt.de/fileadmin/user_upload/editor_common/Policy_Center/SAFE_Policy_White_Paper_74.pdf))

## Jan Marsalek and the limits of the supplied evidence

The requested target includes Jan Marsalek’s disappearance. The supplied materials do not provide a factual account of:

- the date or circumstances of Marsalek’s disappearance;
- his last known location;
- whether he left Germany voluntarily or was assisted;
- his alleged role in Wirecard’s accounting;
- his relationship to the missing €1.9 billion;
- any intelligence, law-enforcement, travel, or financial records concerning him; or
- whether he was suspected, charged, or convicted in relation to the conduct summarized above.

Marsalek is not identified in the supplied Wirecard announcement, and the provided European Parliament study does not include a Marsalek-specific disappearance narrative. Accordingly, no defensible conclusion can be drawn here about his disappearance or personal responsibility. The appropriate finding is **evidentiary absence**, not innocence, guilt, flight, concealment, or death.

## Conclusion

The public record supplied here supports the following concrete opinion: Wirecard’s collapse followed a prolonged failure to resolve credible warnings about its revenues, third-party acquiring arrangements, cash balances, and governance. Wirecard’s 28 April 2020 announcement presented the KPMG review as broadly reassuring, but its own qualifications—and the later account summarized by S2—showed that key historical data and independent confirmation were missing. The decisive issue was not simply that KPMG “found no evidence”; it was that KPMG could not verify essential evidence.

By June 2020, the reported €1.9 billion in trust-account balances were acknowledged by Wirecard’s board as probably nonexistent, EY refused to sign off the 2019 accounts, and the company entered insolvency. The failure was therefore systemic: corporate disclosures, auditing, internal oversight, financial-reporting enforcement, and market supervision did not provide an effective barrier against the alleged fraud.

The Marsalek-disappearance component cannot be reconstructed from the supplied sources. Any attempt to link him to the disappearance or to assign him responsibility for the missing funds would exceed the evidence provided.
